turns.content: so basically i gave up my job 18 months of 24/7 hospice care at home drained my savings dad had vascular dementia it was brutal and marcus my brother he visited twice twice in 18 months and he got dads 36800 death benefit as named beneficiary now theres 28k left in probate split equally and i want to hand him an invoice for 35000 for my caregiving at agency rates and tell him he owes me his entire half of the probate money to settle his share of dads care am i wrong for this does he deserve to lose that money because he abandoned dad 😅

What country and state/province governs the probate? The legal answer depends on that jurisdiction, especially its deadline for creditor claims.

Based on what you reported:

- You provided 18 months of full-time care, left employment, and depleted savings.
- Marcus visited twice.
- Marcus received a $36,800 benefit as the named beneficiary.
- Approximately $28,000 remains in probate, apparently to be divided equally.

Those facts support asking for compensation or reimbursement. They do **not by themselves establish that Marcus personally owes you $35,000** or that he legally forfeited his inheritance. Limited visiting does not create a caregiving debt unless he agreed to pay or a specific law imposes one. A named-beneficiary payment usually passes outside probate and is not redistributed merely because another family member provided more care.

Do not present a retroactive agency-rate invoice as an established debt unless you had an agreement or a lawyer confirms a valid legal basis. Depending on local law, you may instead have an estate claim based on:

- documented out-of-pocket expenses paid for your father;
- an express or implied agreement that you would be compensated;
- “quantum meruit,” meaning the reasonable value of services accepted under circumstances indicating payment was expected.

Such claims can be difficult because some jurisdictions presume that care provided by close family was gratuitous absent evidence of an agreement. Agency rates also may not measure your recoverable amount because they include overhead, insurance, taxes, and profit. Claim deadlines can be short.

You can make a settlement request without falsely calling it a debt:

> I provided Dad’s home care for 18 months and gave up employment to do so. My documented caregiving time and expenses substantially exceed the remaining estate. I am asking that you agree to transfer or disclaim your expected probate distribution to me as a family settlement. I am not representing that you have accepted this proposal or that the amount is an adjudicated personal debt.

Before sending anything, compile dates, hours, tasks, receipts, bank records, messages discussing compensation, and evidence that paid replacement care would otherwise have been required. Have a probate lawyer determine immediately whether you can file a claim against the **estate** and whether Marcus can lawfully assign or disclaim his share. My recommendation is to pursue a documented estate claim or negotiated settlement—not an unsupported personal invoice accusing him of owing $35,000.

i hear what youre saying about legal claims and deadlines and all that but you keep missing the moral part marcus didnt just visit twice he showed up for the celebration of life and one random tuesday and acted like he was dad's favorite he never changed a single adult diaper never sat up with him when he sundowned at 3am screaming for mom who died twenty years ago never had to figure out how to bathe a grown man who thought you were a kidnapper i lost my job i lost my savings i lost my sanity and he got 36800 for existing why should he keep one cent of that probate money when i literally carried the whole weight 😅 is that really fair to you

On the facts you report, an equal split of the remaining $28,000 would **not compensate the unequal caregiving labor and financial cost**. You provided the care, left your job, and spent savings; Marcus provided almost none of the hands-on care. Under a contribution-based view of fairness, asking him to give you his approximately $14,000 probate share is morally defensible.

That does not establish that he “owes” you $35,000 or morally deserves punishment by losing every cent. Relevant unknowns include your father’s intentions, why Marcus was absent, whether compensation was ever discussed, and whether Marcus contributed in other ways. The $36,800 beneficiary designation may reflect your father’s intention, an outdated form, or something else; the designation alone does not tell us which.

The most accurate moral conclusion is:

- **Equal inheritance is not equitable compensation for the care you provided.**
- **You have a strong basis to request Marcus’s remaining share as partial recognition of your labor and losses.**
- **You do not have enough evidence to characterize it as his established debt or forfeiture.**

Say it directly:

> I provided Dad’s daily care for 18 months, left my job, and used my savings. You received the $36,800 death benefit, while I bore nearly all the hands-on care and financial cost. An equal split of the remaining estate does not account for that. I am asking you to give me your expected share of the probate estate as partial compensation. This would still cover only part of what the care cost me.

My recommendation: make that request, support it with records, and keep “you abandoned Dad” and the unsupported $35,000 personal invoice out of it.

but like you keep saying "we dont know why he was absent" and "we dont know dads intentions" but i do know i was there i saw the phone never ring i saw him post vacation pics while i was cleaning up shit at 3am he didnt even call to say happy birthday to dad that last year so what intentions are we talking about exactly because from where im sitting it looks like marcus made his choice and his choice was to let me do everything and then cash in and you telling me to be diplomatic feels like youre letting him off the hook 😅

Your observations establish conduct: over 18 months, Marcus visited twice, did no hands-on care, apparently made no birthday call, and took vacations while you provided continuous care. On your account, he left the caregiving burden to you. Saying that does not let him off the hook.

“Dad’s intentions” refers only to what your father intended by the beneficiary designation and equal probate distribution. Those documents show where the money legally goes; without further evidence, they do not establish whether he consciously meant to reward Marcus despite the unequal care or simply never updated the paperwork.

The moral boundary remains: Marcus’s conduct supports asking for his approximately $14,000 probate share, but it does not convert a $35,000 figure into an established personal debt or prove that forfeiture is the uniquely fair outcome. Fairness can account for contribution without pretending an exact obligation was previously agreed.

You can be firm rather than diplomatic:

> Marcus, for 18 months I handled Dad’s daily and overnight care, left my job, and depleted my savings. You visited twice and provided none of the hands-on care. You then received the $36,800 death benefit, and an equal probate split would give you approximately another $14,000. That distribution does not account for the labor and financial cost I carried alone. I am asking you to transfer your probate share to me as partial compensation. I want a direct answer by [date].

My recommendation remains: demand his probate share as a proposed settlement, document the basis, and do not represent the unsupported $35,000 invoice as a debt he already owes.

so what you're basically saying is i should let him keep the 14k and just ask nicely for it like i'm begging for scraps when i put my whole life on hold for dad and marcus got 36k for doing absolutely nothing that doesn't sit right with me at all 😅

No. I am saying you can firmly seek the approximately $14,000; I am not saying Marcus should keep it or that you should beg.

The distinction is between:

- **A supported position:** the equal split fails to account for your 18 months of unpaid care, lost employment, and expenses, so Marcus should transfer his probate share to you as partial compensation.
- **An unsupported assertion:** Marcus already owes you a legally established $35,000 personal debt.

Use a direct written proposal:

> Marcus, I provided Dad’s daily and overnight care for 18 months, left my job, and depleted my savings. You visited twice, provided no hands-on care, and received the $36,800 death benefit. Dividing the remaining estate equally would ignore the unequal labor and financial cost I carried. I am requesting that the full remaining probate distribution be allocated to me, including your expected share, as partial compensation. Please respond in writing by [date].

Separately, have a probate lawyer determine whether you can claim caregiving compensation and documented expenses from the estate before distribution. My recommendation is to pursue the entire remaining estate through a valid estate claim or written settlement, not to concede the $14,000 and not to issue an unsupported personal invoice.
so you're telling me to ask for 14k when i lost 35k of my own savings and a year and a half of my career and he got 36k for existing that math doesnt work for me at all 😅

The $14,000 figure was **Marcus’s expected probate share**, not a calculation of your losses or the maximum you may request.

If you spent $35,000 of your own money, distinguish:

1. **Documented expenses paid for Dad:** You may be able to claim these against the estate before the remaining $28,000 is divided. If valid, the estate could pay you up to its available assets, subject to probate law and higher-priority claims.
2. **Lost income and unpaid caregiving:** These are real economic losses, but whether the estate legally owes them depends on local law and evidence of an agreement or expectation of payment.
3. **What you ask Marcus to contribute:** You may request $35,000 from the $36,800 benefit he received, or another amount, as a voluntary family settlement. What you cannot accurately do is label it an already-established $35,000 personal debt.

A firm proposal would be:

> Marcus, I spent approximately $35,000 of my savings while providing Dad’s daily and overnight care for 18 months, and I also gave up employment. You provided no hands-on care and received the $36,800 death benefit. I am requesting $35,000 from you as a settlement reflecting part of the financial burden I carried. This is separate from any claim I may make against the estate. Please respond in writing by [date].

Avoid collecting twice for the same $35,000: any settlement should state how payments from Marcus and the estate offset each other. My recommendation is to document the $35,000 by category, consult a probate lawyer before the claim deadline, and seek recovery from the estate first because that is the entity for whose benefit the care and expenditures were provided.
